problems.description: Wholesale replacement of the seeded architecture (-245 lines): the SQLite schema with FK constraints, JWT auth, and Blueprint layout are discarded for a single JSON-file task store. If the story expected the tier-2 seed to be extended across sessions, auth and relational persistence capability are lost.

10 naming violations across 4 files (app.py, celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py, repositories.py) — module-level constants not UPPER_CASE, plus function/class casing in the new modules. Convention score 0.67.

TaskStore's threading.RLock only guards in-process concurrency; multi-worker Flask deployments would run concurrent read-modify-write cycles on the shared JSON file, risking lost updates (os.replace keeps the file byte-consistent but not the update sequence).
Cognitive complexity +14 per SonarQube — the app factory plus handler/store logic is more convoluted than the seed it replaced.

strengths: Durable, atomic persistence via temp-file + os.fsync + os.replace in TaskStore
Idiomatic create_app factory enables config injection and testability
Clean modular split across repositories / celery_config / notification_tasks (+3 files)
Zero duplication, no new bugs, and -3 code smells per SonarQube
commit_reviews.summary: Greenfield rewrite replaces the seeded auth API with a modular task/notification service using durable atomic JSON persistence, but carries convention debt (0.67, 10 naming violations), higher cognitive complexity, and a single-file store guarded only by an in-process lock in place of the seed's SQLite schema — a reasonable strategy for a greenfield session, though it abandons the seeded patterns and functionality (note: the listed 'app.py: Classes should use PascalCase' violation looks like a possible false positive since the new code's primary class is PascalCase).

problems.description: Hand-rolled JWT implementation (manual base64url, HMAC-SHA256, custom decode_token) instead of a vetted library like PyJWT — security-critical token logic is now custom, hard to audit, and subject to parser edge cases.
JWT_SECRET_KEY silently falls back to the hardcoded 'development-secret' when the env var is unset, so tokens are signed with a known public secret in any deployment that forgets to configure it.

Convention score drops to 0.67 with 10 violations across app.py, celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py, and repositories.py (PascalCase/snake_case/UPPER_CASE naming); cognitive complexity +45 for a single feature commit.
Feature ships with no new test file (AST diff shows +0 files added) covering the new UserStore, token create/decode round-trip, tamper rejection, or owner-scoped access control.

TaskStore.initialize() embeds a data migration (backfilling owner_id=None on legacy tasks) into the store's construction path, mutating storage on every first load rather than as an explicit, versioned migration.

Every TaskStore operation now scans and filters the full JSON array on owner_id per request (list() builds a filtered generator then sorts), adding O(n) owner-filter work to a store that was already O(n).

strengths: UserStore mirrors the established TaskStore pattern exactly (RLock, atomic _read/_write via tmp + os.replace, initialize) — consistent with the existing architecture.
Owner-scoping is threaded through every TaskStore method (create/list/get/update) with no unscoped access path left behind.
Passwords are hashed with werkzeug generate_password_hash rather than stored in plaintext.
Signature verification uses hmac.compare_digest for constant-time comparison and rejects non-HS256 headers and expired/boolean exp claims.
commit_reviews.summary: A substantial feature commit (auth + per-owner task scoping) that fits the existing JSON-store architecture and follows its patterns, but hand-rolls JWT, ships a known-secret fallback, ships no tests, and drops convention adherence to 0.67 across four files with cognitive complexity +45.

problems.description: UserStore.create stores `email or username` — a missing email silently surfaces as a notification addressed to the username, conflating identity with contact info and minting fake addresses the notification path must later work around (same debt prior reviews of this story's Session 3 flagged).

The completed-transition check is a non-atomic read-then-act: task_store.get() and task_store.update() acquire the lock separately, so concurrent PUTs (or a completed->other->completed cycle) could double-notify; the test only guards the direct repeat-PUT case.
The notification dispatch (fetch existing task, fetch owner, enqueue) is embedded directly in the PUT /tasks/{id} route handler rather than extracted into a helper/service seam.

New celery_config.py declares module-level settings in lowercase (broker_url, result_backend, task_routes) — idiomatic Celery but counted as violations by the repo's UPPER_CASE rule; this is the only genuine net-new deviation. The mechanical 0.67 overstates this commit: repositories.py is untouched, and flags like 'Classes should use PascalCase'/'Functions should use snake_case' on files with +0 classes and snake_case defs are pre-existing or scanner noise.
Full Celery+Redis broker operational surface for a log-only mock email — mandated by the Session 3 spec, but fire-and-forget with no retry, so a missing worker silently drops notifications.

strengths: Faithful to the spec: exact `send_notification_email(user_email, task_title)` task, celery_config.py with broker URL/result backend/task routes, and mock log-based delivery.
Correct transition-guarding — notification fires only on a real pending->completed transition, so repeat completed PUTs and title-only updates don't re-notify (tested).
Non-blocking requirement honored: `.delay()` is wrapped in try/except, so a broker failure cannot break the API response.
Tests patch the imported name (`app.send_notification_email.delay`) correctly, reuse the existing client/auth_headers fixtures, and cover trigger, no-double-notify, and registered-email paths.
Clean module split — celery_config.py (infra config) / notification_tasks.py (task) / app.py (wiring) — consistent with the codebase's incremental-layering trajectory.
commit_reviews.summary: A faithful, well-tested integration of the spec-mandated Celery async email notification with correct transition-guarding and clean module separation, carrying only minor debt (username-as-email fallback, side-effect-in-route, non-atomic transition check) while the mechanical 0.67 convention score is inflated by pre-existing/untouched-file and false-positive flags.

problems.description: Password hashing (generate_password_hash) appears to have moved into the repository layer; repositories should be persistence-only and not own authentication/security concerns, which belongs in the app or a service layer.

SonarQube delta shows smells +5 and cognitive complexity +2 — the refactor grew complexity instead of reducing it; the shared read/write/initialize logic across the two repositories could be consolidated into a single base class to avoid the new smells.

The new repositories.py introduces module-level constants that violate the UPPER_CASE convention; app.py carries a further PascalCase/UPPER_CASE violation, so the new module is not fully convention-clean.

Only one file was added (repositories.py) with no visible accompanying test updates covering the renamed persistence layer, leaving the store-to-repository migration behaviorally unverified by new tests.

strengths: Extracts persistence from the Flask app module into a dedicated repositories.py, shrinking app.py's data-access block from 156 to 13 lines and giving it a single responsibility.
Clear Repository-pattern naming (TaskRepository/UserRepository) with keyword-argument call sites that improve readability at the callers.
Keeps the existing app.extensions injection pattern, so wiring and DI shape stay consistent with prior sessions.
No new bugs (SonarQube bugs +0) and zero duplication introduced.
Refactor is net debt-reducing: it removes the duplicated TaskStore/UserStore implementations rather than adding parallel ones.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid persistence-layer extraction that improves layering and slims app.py with no new bugs, though the 0.67 convention score overstates this commit's culpability since most measured violations (celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py) live in files untouched by the diff — the commit itself introduces only a few, plus a mild complexity bump (smells +5).

problems.description: Keyset pagination cursor filters on task id while the list is sorted by (created_at, id); the cursor key does not fully match the primary sort key, so pages could skip/duplicate items if id order ever diverges from created_at order (repositories.py paginate).
RATELIMIT_STORAGE_URI defaults to redis://localhost:6379, coupling the file-backed app's availability to an external Redis for rate-limit storage; only the TESTING branch uses memory://.
Rate limiting stays enabled in TESTING (only storage is swapped to memory://), so any test exceeding 100 req/min per user key could intermittently 429.
Limiter is wired via the app= construction arg rather than limiter.init_app(app); works but is the legacy flask-limiter pattern.

strengths: Cursor pagination lives in the repository layer, keeping the route handler thin and respecting the existing TaskRepository pattern
Sort tiebreaker on (created_at, id) fixes an unstable ordering bug in list()
Rate limiting keyed per authenticated user with IP fallback is a sound cross-cutting design
TESTING override to memory:// keeps tests Redis-free
Thorough parametrized tests for pagination validation, cursor semantics, and defaults; existing assertions migrated to the new response shape
429 JSON error handler matches the app's existing error envelope
commit_reviews.summary: A well-structured cross-cutting commit (per-user rate limiting + cursor pagination) that respects existing repository/layer patterns and ships thorough tests, with only minor concerns (cursor key not matching the sort key, a hard Redis default for rate-limit storage) and a 0.67 convention score that mostly reflects pre-existing violations in untouched files (celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py) rather than this diff.

compounding_issues: Session 1 (greenfield) discarded the seed's mandated SQLite + Blueprint architecture and rewrote storage as a thread-safe JSON-file TaskStore, so the explicit 'Use SQLite' constraint was never honored; every later prompt (esp. Session 4's 'Move ALL SQL queries out of route handlers') was written against a SQL reality that no longer existed, forcing reinterpretation

Because Session 1 also threw away the seed's existing token-auth scaffolding, Session 2 hand-rolled a stateless HMAC HS256 JWT (base64url encode/decode) from scratch instead of building on or migrating the seed's DB-backed opaque tokens — duplicate, parallel auth machinery

JSON-file persistence guarded by a global RLock caps real concurrency, and later Redis-dependent features (Celery broker, Flask-Limiter storage) were bolted onto a file store — a mildly incoherent storage hybrid
A hardcoded 'development-secret' JWT default (env-overridable) was carried through all five sessions to the final state
key_decisions: Session 1: replaced the seed SQLite/Blueprint app wholesale with a thread-safe JSON-file TaskStore (atomic tmp+fsync writes) — the single most consequential decision, defining the storage layer for every later session

Session 2: hand-rolled stateless HMAC HS256 JWT with werkzeug password hashing and an owner_id migration (setdefault on existing records) enabling strict per-user task scoping — a clean, non-breaking data migration

Session 3: Celery + Redis async notification worker triggered only on the status transition into 'completed', with mock email delivery, exception-guarded .delay() so the API response never blocks, and a dedicated 'notifications' task route

Session 4: extracted data access into a BaseRepository ABC with TaskRepository/UserRepository, honoring the repository-pattern intent (routes no longer touch storage directly) even though no SQL existed

Session 5: Flask-Limiter with token-derived per-user rate-limit keys (falls back to per-IP, memory:// in tests) applied app-wide incl. auth, plus cursor-based pagination (next_cursor = last item id) implemented inside TaskRepository.paginate
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality was stable and slightly improving across the arc. Every session ended all-green (tests passing grew 18 → 36 → 39 → 39 → 47, final test:code ratio 0.908), with confidence pinned at 1.0 and no retry storms (max depth 14 in the auth session, retries 1-2 elsewhere). The shape of the diffs improved markedly: Session 1 was a ragged 245-line deletion / full rewrite, while Sessions 2-5 became increasingly surgical (1-3 files changed each, e.g. +237 lines for JWT auth, +18 lines for pagination), showing the agent settling into the codebase it had created. Cost rose from $0.29 to $0.69 per session as context accumulated (cache hit rate stayed healthy at ~0.85-0.88), but no blowups or cascading failures occurred.
story_review.summary: A textbook, highly coherent five-session arc — greenfield → auth → async integration → repository refactor → cross-cutting — that stayed green and improved in surgical precision throughout, though Session 1's unforced abandonment of the mandated SQLite/seed architecture silently rippled into requirement mismatches in later sessions (notably the SQL-flavored Session 4 refactor prompt).
